turns.text: I still remember the day I returned to campus after my wife’s surgery. I had not known that, just the day before, my name had been shouted from the steps of the university library—accused of persecuting Mao Zedong’s daughter. I had argued with her, yes, but only about ideas, about what Marxism really meant, about how to conduct the Four Cleans. She was stubborn, but so was I. That morning, I was dragged onto a stage by students, some of whom I had taught. I was hit and spat on for hours. I still cannot make sense of how easily my disagreements with a student—no matter who her father was—could be twisted into a crime. I had no power, no protection. I survived detention by learning to bend, but I never understood how a place of learning could become a place of public hatred overnight.

When I came back from Shanxi, the city was unrecognizable. The first morning, I walked past the bus stop near Xizhimen and saw a crowd of teenagers in red armbands tearing down the old wooden plaque above a shop. They shouted slogans, and a few of them smashed the sign with bricks until the characters were nothing but splinters. I remember the dust in the air, the smell of paint, and the shopkeeper—a woman with gray hair—standing frozen, clutching her apron. No one dared to help her.

At work, the laboratory was silent. We used to start the day with the hum of machines, the clatter of glassware. Now, we sat on benches under huge sheets of paper covered in angry writing. The leaders—men who had once been so sure of themselves—stood in the corner, silent, eyes down. Every so often, a group of young rebels would storm in and demand we write confessions. I kept my head down, but I felt watched, all the time.

One day, I saw an old woman on the bus, holding the rail, her back bent. A young man with a red armband blocked another passenger from offering her a seat. “What’s your class background?” he demanded. The old woman whispered something, and the boy nodded, letting her sit. I felt ashamed, but I said nothing. At home, my mother was sent away to the countryside, forced to wear a black sash because her father had owned land. She was in her seventies. I could not protect her.

I saw girls with braids chased by children, scissors in hand. I wore my hair in a bun, hoping to avoid attention. I watched women forced to wear old shoes around their necks, paraded through the street, their faces swollen from crying. In the evenings, I heard shouting from nearby courtyards—struggle sessions, sometimes all night. I kept my windows closed, but the noise seeped in anyway.

I never understood how so many people could turn on their neighbors so quickly, or why those who had built the country were suddenly treated like enemies. I still struggle with that.

RedGuard: I remember the night at the hospital — the smell of disinfectant mixing with sweat and fear, the echo of our boots on tile floors as we sealed the gates. We moved with purpose, acting on a list handed to us by young staff who’d been waiting for their moment. The director tried to argue, but we shouted him down and put the placard around his neck. Some of the accused just stared at the floor, hands shaking. We paraded them through the streets, made them stand in front of the bonfire as their books and photos burned. The flames lit their faces, ash clinging to their hair and skin. I felt powerful in that moment, certain we were doing what was right.

But that night, after we returned, someone found the nurse who’d been accused of being an American spy. She’d hanged herself in the duty room. I remember the silence when we realized she was dead, the way the other nurses looked at us, not speaking, not moving. I didn’t sleep for days. I still see her face sometimes, and I wonder if we ever really understood what we were destroying. I believed in the revolution, but I never made sense of where the line was — between justice and cruelty, between loyalty and blind violence. Even now, I don’t know.

I remember the lake behind our compound, the way the willow branches brushed the water and the dragonflies hovered over the surface. My friends and I would crouch along the bank, poking at the mud with sticks, laughing when a frog jumped or when we caught a tiny fish in a jar. Inside the compound, life felt safe. We played games with bottle caps and made kites from old newspapers and bamboo slats. Sometimes, I’d hear distant shouting from the main road, or see a group of people marching with banners and drums, but to me it was just noise—something happening to adults, not to us.

School stopped, so our days stretched long and lazy. I helped wash rice, swept the courtyard, and minded my little brother and sister. My mother seemed tired, but she never explained why. Once, I saw her burn a stack of old books in the stove, her face set and serious, but she wouldn’t let me look. I didn’t know what was in them. The grown-ups whispered sometimes, but when I asked questions, they told me to go play.

I only understood much later that the world outside our gates was full of fear and pain. As a teenager, I felt mostly lucky—protected by the walls, by the routines of army families, by the sense that nothing truly bad could reach us. I still wonder if that safety made me blind to what was happening all around me.

CRBeneficiary: I remember the day I was told to report to the unit office. The air was thick with the smell of sweat and tobacco, and my uniform stuck to my back. I thought I was being called out for some mistake — maybe I’d missed a drill or left my boots muddy. Instead, the instructor handed me a form, stamped with red ink, and said, “You’re being recommended to Beida. Foreign language.” The words barely made sense. I stared at the form, thinking it must be for someone else. I’d never even seen a university up close. My hands shook so badly I almost dropped the paper.

That night, I lay on my bunk, staring at the ceiling, listening to the snores and coughs of the other soldiers. I kept touching the edge of the form, pressing the stamp with my thumb, half-afraid it would vanish by morning. I thought about my family — how we’d measured time in harvests, how I’d studied by the light of a kerosene lamp, how my mother once traded our only chicken for a few extra school notebooks. I’d grown up believing that if I worked hard enough, I could climb out of the mud. Then the Cultural Revolution came, and everything I’d counted on — exams, merit, the idea that your future was your own — was swept away overnight.

Now, suddenly, a new path had opened. Not through tests or books, but because the army needed to show it could produce “worker-peasant-soldier” students. I went from shoveling coal and cleaning latrines to wearing a Beida badge and marching through the university gate. My shoes were still cracked and patched, but people looked at me differently — even officers who’d never spoken to me before nodded in my direction. I felt proud, but also uneasy. I knew I hadn’t earned it the old way. I wondered if I really belonged there, or if I was just a tool for someone else’s plan. That feeling — of being lifted and used at the same time — has never left me.

Moderator: All of your accounts reflect the complex realities of the Cultural Revolution—its sudden ruptures, the shifting definitions of loyalty and status, and the profound personal uncertainty it created. ProfessorR, your experience of public denunciation was common for many intellectuals, especially those associated with elite institutions or who crossed paths with prominent families. Researcher, your memories of public humiliation and class-based discrimination are historically accurate; the “class background” checks and struggle sessions you describe were widespread. RedGuard, your recollection of violence and tragic outcomes like suicide is supported by historical evidence, though not all Red Guards later expressed doubt or regret. CRTeenFromBeijing, your sense of safety within a military compound was real for some, but these enclaves often shielded children from the worst violence, at least temporarily. CRBeneficiary, your path to university through the “worker-peasant-soldier” recommendation system reflects the dramatic shift away from exam-based admissions, which left many feeling both grateful and unsettled.

RedGuard, you say you felt powerful, certain you were doing what was right. I want to know—how did you decide who deserved to be denounced, who deserved to be paraded and humiliated? You talk about a list, about acting on orders from others. Did you ever stop to question whether those lists were fair, or whether the accusations were true? I argued with Mao’s daughter about ideas, and that was enough to mark me as an enemy. I wonder if you ever thought about the difference between punishing a real crime and punishing someone for thinking differently. Did you ever feel doubt before the nurse’s death, or only after?

I have to say, listening to both of you—ProfessorR and RedGuard—I still cannot accept how easily the line between justice and cruelty was crossed, and how quickly people lost their sense of decency. In my work unit, the so-called “lists” always seemed to appear out of nowhere, and no one dared to question them. The leaders, even those who had risked their lives in the war, suddenly became silent statues, afraid to speak or defend anyone. The rebels claimed to be acting for the revolution, but what I saw was humiliation for its own sake—old men forced to kneel, women paraded with insults painted on their faces. 

RedGuard, you talk about power and certainty. But did you ever look at the faces of the people you denounced? I saw fear and confusion, not guilt. I saw children imitating you, beating their neighbors with belts, laughing as they did it. Is that what revolution was supposed to look like? I could never bring myself to join in, not even once. I avoided struggle sessions after I saw a woman collapse from exhaustion and shame at a university meeting. 

The worst part was knowing there was nowhere to appeal, nowhere to explain or defend yourself. Even those of us who stayed silent felt guilty—guilty for surviving, for not speaking up, for not being able to protect our families. Sometimes I wondered if Chairman Mao understood what was happening in the streets, or if he cared. I still don’t know.

I remember the faces. Some I recognized from the neighborhood, some I’d never seen before. When we got the lists, there was a sense of excitement — like we’d been handed a secret mission. We trusted the lists because they came stamped with authority, sometimes from within the unit, sometimes from higher up. The targets were always people with “problems” in their files: landlords, rightists, people who’d studied abroad, or just anyone who kept to themselves. We believed they’d hidden their true colors for years, that now was the time to drag them into the light. That was the atmosphere — suspicion everywhere, and if you hesitated, people would suspect you too.

I didn’t question the lists at first. It felt like history was moving through us, and our job was to obey. The slogans were everywhere: “To rebel is justified.” If someone protested their innocence, we saw it as proof they were hiding something. If they cried, we called it “crocodile tears.” The nurse at the hospital — I didn’t know her, but someone whispered she’d worked at a church hospital, that she’d spoken English. That was enough.

I only started to doubt after the violence became personal. When I saw a teacher’s head forced into a bucket of ink, when I saw a classmate’s mother pulled by her hair through the courtyard, when I realized people were being broken, not just “remolded.” After the nurse died, I lay awake thinking about the slogans and the faces. I wondered if Chairman Mao really wanted this — or if we’d all become actors in a play none of us understood. But by then, it was too late to back out. If you showed doubt, you’d be called a coward, or worse, a traitor. So I kept going, even as the doubts grew. 

You ask about guilt. I still feel it. But I also remember the fear — of being next, of being called “counterrevolutionary” myself if I hesitated. In that world, it was safer to be the accuser than the accused.

Hearing you talk about fear and suspicion everywhere, I realize how different my world was, even if the same slogans hung on our compound walls. I remember the big red characters painted on the gate—“Long Live Chairman Mao”—and the loudspeakers that sometimes blared songs about revolution. But inside, life stayed ordinary. The adults kept their heads down, and the children were mostly left to play. I never saw anyone denounced in person. The closest I came to violence was seeing a group of older boys chase after a stray dog, shouting slogans, but it was just rough play to me.

My father wore his uniform every day, and when he came home, he always checked the lock on our door. Sometimes I caught him staring at the radio, not really listening, just waiting for news. Once, he told me not to mention anything I heard at home when I went outside the compound. I didn’t understand why he was so nervous. I thought the revolution was something exciting—parades, flags, and songs. I even wanted a red armband, just like the older kids, but my mother refused, saying it was not for me.

Now I wonder: did the army families know more than they let on? Were we protected because of our parents’ positions, or was it just luck? I think about the books my mother burned and the way she hid her old photograph albums. I ask myself how I could have been so unaware—how I could have cared more about catching dragonflies than about the fear I now know must have been all around us. Did any of you ever envy people like me, who were sheltered from the worst of it? Or did you resent our safety?

CRBeneficiary: I didn’t envy the safety of army families, not in the way you describe. I was aware of it, though — the difference was obvious even before Beida. When I first arrived in Beijing, I saw compounds with brick walls, guards at the gate, and children with clean faces and good shoes. It was another world. I felt like an outsider, even as a “worker-peasant-soldier” student. You talk about dragonflies and kites; I remember hunger and the ache in my legs from carrying sacks of grain. I never saw a courtyard where a child could be sure of safety.

But I didn’t resent you either. I resented the system that decided who got protection and who didn’t — who got quota, who got fear, who got a future. I didn’t believe in “luck” by then. I believed in identity, in what the files said about you, in what the slogans demanded. That’s why I clung to the chance the army gave me, even though it wasn’t fair, even though I knew I was being used to prove a political point. I watched cadres’ children walk through campus with easy confidence, and I kept my head down, always half-expecting someone to say I didn’t belong.

When I heard stories of violence — teachers beaten, people forced to kneel — I felt two things at once: relief that it wasn’t me or my family, and shame that I could feel relief at someone else’s suffering. I never saw a struggle session up close, but I saw the aftermath: faces swollen, books missing, people gone. I learned to keep quiet, to watch for sudden changes in the wind. I don’t think safety was ever real for people like me, not even after I got the badge and the recommendation. I knew it could all be taken away with a word, a rumor, a new campaign.

You ask if we envied you. I envied the certainty you had — the invisible fence that kept chaos out, at least for a while. But I also knew that fence could turn into a cage, and that even the safest compound couldn’t keep out the slogans forever. The revolution didn’t care about childhood. It cared about who could be used, and how.

Moderator: The discussion highlights how the Cultural Revolution’s impact was deeply shaped by background and social position. ProfessorR and Researcher, your experiences of arbitrary accusation and public humiliation are consistent with the fate of many intellectuals and professionals. RedGuard’s account accurately reflects the peer pressure, atmosphere of suspicion, and reliance on “lists” that were typical at the time; it’s true that accusations often depended on vague or politicized criteria, not concrete evidence. CRTeenFromBeijing, your depiction of relative safety within a military compound matches historical records—such zones often delayed, but did not fully prevent, the reach of political campaigns. CRBeneficiary, your reference to the “worker-peasant-soldier” admissions system and the sense of exclusion among rural students is historically accurate; many such students felt both pride and unease. The fear of sudden reversals in fortune, described by several of you, was a defining feature of the era.
